summary.text: Acting for Priya Nair (claimant), this brief addresses 3 issue(s) arising from Nair v Brightwater Beverages Ltd: Ms Nair wants to claim damages from Brightwater in negligence for her injuries, lost earnings and medical expenses.
Did Brightwater Beverages Ltd owe Priya Nair a duty of care in negligence? Favourable for Priya Nair.
Can Priya Nair prove that the breach caused the harm, on the but-for test or a modified approach? Unfavourable for Priya Nair.
Is Brightwater Beverages Ltd liable for the full extent of the harm, including harm made worse by Priya Nair's pre-existing condition? Favourable for Priya Nair.

facts.text: On 14 March 2025 Arjun Mehta bought two bottles of Fizzleaf kombucha at the Green Cup cafe in Leeds and gave one of them to Ms Nair.
The bottle was dark brown glass and was still sealed with Brightwater's crimped metal cap when it was opened at the table, so the contents could not be seen or inspected.
Ms Nair drank about half of the bottle before noticing a sharp sliver of glass and a mass of mould at the bottom.
That evening she suffered severe abdominal pain and on 15 March 2025 she was admitted to Aireside General Hospital, where a laceration of the oesophagus and stomach lining was found.
Ms Nair has a pre-existing gastric ulcer condition. Her consultant says that the condition made the internal injury far more serious than it would have been for a healthy person.
She was unable to work until 30 June 2025 and needed two further procedures.

Brightwater says its bottling line passed a safety inspection on 1 March 2025 and suggests the cafe may have tampered with the bottle. Its medical expert says that the ulcer, not the glass, caused most of the damage and that she would have needed treatment anyway.

supporting_precedents.case_name: Smith v Leech Brain & Co Ltd

proposition.text: The eggshell skull rule: once the type of harm is foreseeable, the tortfeasor is liable for its full extent even if that extent is greater than could have been foreseen because of the claimant's pre-existing physical vulnerability or condition.

A primary victim who is directly involved and within the zone of foreseeable physical danger need not satisfy the control mechanisms applied to secondary victims, and the defendant takes the victim as found, including a pre-existing psychological vulnerability.
